full_judgment:
12. The suit land is, no doubt, char land and agricultural in nature which invokes sections 76 and 81 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act being the relevant law for the purpose of settlement of the suit land by way of lease. Section 81(b) has been incorporated in 1971 by amending State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 Section 76(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as under: 

 Section 81 (b) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is as follows: 

 "Registration of lease deed. Notwithstanding anything contained in sections 81 and 81A or any other law for the time being in force, no agricultural or non-agricultural tenancy shall in law be created or deemed to have been created, even after acceptance of salami and/or rent from the lessee, till a deed of lease has been executed in favour of the lessee by an authority competent to grant lease of Government khas land or any other Gazetted Officer duly authorized in this behalf and the said lease has been duly registered under the provision of clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908." 

 15. On the other hand, Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the defendants opposite parties, submits that the lease was completed. Only for shortage of execution of the lease deed which is a mereformality as the plaintiff was given possession and the plaintiff made liable for payment of compensation by Exhibit.2 series it cannot be said that the lease was not valid one. Mr. Momtazuddin, further submits that only because of pendency of the present litigation necessary deed could not executed and registered. According to him, compliance of section 81(b) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is there. Mr. Momtazuddin also submits that, a declaration of title as prayed for by the plaintiff is not a bar because of section 76(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 "All previous proposals for settlement of agricultural khas lands at whatever stages they may be, except where the lease deed has already been executed and registered, should be cancelled and the lands covered by such proposals should be leased out in accordance with the provisions of this Government order. In this connection section 81B of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, may be referred to." 

 18. My considered opinion is that the GO or the said clause have not taken away in any manner the force and the meaning of section 81 (b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Neither in the said GO nor in the implementation clause anything is there which can supersede the precise and clear prohibition of section 81(b) of the said Act which must be complied, while leasing out agricultural khas land, as in the present case. 

 19. Here, in this case, whatever may be approval or proposal the settlement of the suit land was not complete as the lease deed as required under section 81 (b) has not been effected. Section 76(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as under: 

 20. Mr. Momtazuddin, the learned Counsel; cites a decision in the case of Abdul Majid and others vs Province of East Pakistan and others reported in 23 DLR 203. But that case was decided before the enactment of section 81(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that case judgment was passed on 1st May, 1970. So that one is not applicable in the case Quayum, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, cites the decision in the case of Benzir Ahmed vs Debendra Chandra Saha and others, reported in 4 BLT J 50, wherein the Appellate Division held in para 3 that in a suit for declaration of title mere possession of the property is not sufficient unless the plaintiff can produce a document of title showing his acquisition of right, title and interest in the suit property. 

 22. The appellate Court has not considered this vital and legal aspect of the case invoking sections 81(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Appellate Court also failed to appreciate that in this case the alleged settlement was made after 1971 and not before that Appellate Court also failed to appreciate the evidence on record that the settlement to the plaintiff was in the .nature of a proposal and its approval has not been concluded. So, the revenue authority was quite competent to cancel the same being the highest and appropriate authority. The order directing the plaintiff to give back the possession of the suit land to the Government is legal and it is maintained. The plaintiff must give back possession of the suit land to the Government, if not by this time. The suit property can be settled to the genuine persons and claimants afresh in accordance with law.
